Super Sidekicks 2: The World Championship is the sequel corrected most of the flaws in the original's design, including the ability to switch players' control during the game, a smaller goal, and no more long shots taken. The game increased the number of teams to 48 and divided them into 6 geographical regions:
 - Europe A: Italy, England, Spain, Holland, Switzerland, Norway, Turkey and Ireland.
 - Europe B: Germany, France, Bulgaria, Sweden, Russia, Greece, Belgium and Romania.
 - Americas/Oceania: United States, Mexico, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Costa Rica, El Salvador and Honduras.
 - Asia: South Korea, Japan, Saudi Arabia, Taiwan (as Republic of China), China, Iran, Hong Kong and United Arab Emirates.
 - South America: Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, Colombia, Bolivia, Uruguay, Peru and Ecuador.
 - Africa: Cameroon, Morocco, Nigeria, Egypt, South Africa, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea and Zambia.
Super Sidekicks 3: The Next Glory

Super Sidekicks 3: The Next Glory is an arcade style soccer/football game, continuation of Super Sidekicks 2: The World Championship. The game features 64 national teams (across 8 regions.)

Like its predecessor, Super Sidekicks 3: The Next Glory is a soccer game that is played from a top-down perspective in a two-dimensional environment with sprites. Though it follows the same gameplay as with other soccer titles at the time and most of the sport's rules are present, the game opts for a more arcade-styled approach of the sport instead of being full simulation. New features in this game include naming the player scoring goals for his team and keeping score of how many goals he scores during his team's use by the player. Alongside the "Top Teams" ranking which serves as a high score table for teams, there is a "Top Scorer" table for individual players. The name and use of scoring players is random.
Super Slam

In Super Slam, up to four players play tennis matches in either singles or doubles. If players choose to play alone against computer controlled A.I. opponents there is a set time limit. Once that time limit has expired players must use another credits if they want to continue the game.
Super Soccer
Coin-op version of the classic Super Famicom soccer game.
Super Spacefortress Macross

Super Spacefortress Macross is a vertically-scrolling shoot'em up based on the 1984 theatrical film in the Macross franchise, commonly known in English as Macross: Do You Remember Love?. Players control the VF-1 Valkyrie fighters of ace pilots Max Jenius and (in two-player games only) Hikaru Ichijyo in combat against the Zentradi.

The game consists of seven levels, mostly based on action scenes from the film, including confrontations over Macross City, in the rings of Saturn, the surface of the devastated Earth, and the final battle against Boddole Zer.

Gameplay is similar to Raiden: the Valkyrie can transform into one of three different modes by collecting the appropriate power-up: in Fighter mode, the ship fires a spread shot, Gerwalk mode has a narrow but powerful laser that passes through enemies, and Battroid mode features homing missiles. The intensity of the attacks can be upgraded in three stages through another power-up.
Super Spacefortress Macross II

In 1999, an alien ship crashes on South Atalia Island and makes the human race aware of other life in space. Ten years later, the ship is reconstructed and christened as the SDF-1 Macross. However, on the day of its maiden voyage, an alien race called the Zentraedi make their appearance on Earth, beginning the UN Spacy/Zentraedi war that would change the history of both races forever.
Super Special Criminal Investigation

Player controlled two cops, the first would drive a Nissan 300ZX T-Top Turbo in pursuit of the suspect vehicles, and the second would stand up in the passenger seat and fire upon the enemy cars, when the player pressed one of the steering wheel's trigger buttons.
Super Speed Race

Super Speed Race is the successor to Racer. The game features sprites for cars in a top down view. The player's car is controlled with a steering wheel attached to the arcade cabinet, an accelerator and gear shift. The player's speed is shown on a separate speedometer rather than on-screen. The racing track scrolls, continues straight ahead, and features color scenery graphics on either side. The high scores of the best five players are stored and displayed on a separate LED display to the left of the screen.
Super Speed Race Jr.

Super Speed Race Jr. is a racing arcade game that was released by Taito Corporation in 1985 only in Japan; it is the seventh and final title in their Speed Race series. The player must use a steering wheel to take up control of a car, with a single pedal to make it accelerate. The car in question is coloured red and you must guide it through the streets of a city while avoiding other CPU-controlled cars (one of which is a yellow Volkswagen Buggy), and trying not to go off the road; you will also have to watch out for zebra and level crossings as pedestrians and diesel-hauled trains pass over them.
Super Speed Race V

Super Speed Race V is a racing arcade game which was released by Taito Corporation in 1978; it is the fourth title in their Speed Race series, and the "V" stands for the game's five best scorers (shown on the LED displays to the left of the monitor, above the player score and timer). The player must yet again utilize a steering wheel and gear shifter, to take up control of a car, with a single pedal to make it accelerate - and this time, the gameplay will be extended at 3000 points, while the old "Slip Zones" from the first two "SR" games will appear on the track at 800 points and every 1000 points thereafter.
Super Sprint

Super Sprint is a racing game for one or two players, with the Arcade version allowing three players to race at the same time. Gameplay is from an overhead view of the racetrack. The racetracks start simple and gradually get more complicated, and may also feature obstacles ranging from traffic cones to tornadoes. Occasionally wrenches will appear in the roadway, and when collected they can be used after a race to power up your car with better tires, better acceleration or a higher top speed.
Super Star Crest

Super Star Crest is a classic fixed-screen arcade shoot-'em-up from the early 1980s, widely recognized as an authorized clone or bootleg variant of Nichibutsu's seminal title, Moon Cresta. It was manufactured by Taito do Brasil under license, bringing the multi-stage docking space shooter to the South American market.
Super Stingray

A semi-strategic top-down tank action shooter game.

Control your tank across the battlefield and destroy all the enemies in the way and defeated the enemy fortress.
Super Streak

The Super Streak is a classic UK pub fruit machine manufactured by Barcrest, one of the most iconic names in the British amusement industry. Built on the highly influential Dx01/MPU hardware generation, the machine features an £8 jackpot profile (historically varying by venue setup or specific era conversions). It is highly regarded among enthusiasts of traditional multi-feature AWPs (Amusement with Prizes) for its reliance on the classic "streak" mechanic.

Unlike basic machines that reset after a big payout, Super Streak is built to deliver multiple back-to-back wins. When a player forces or lands the core "Super Streak" feature, the machine enters a hyper-active profile mode where it regularly dishes out consecutive nudges, repeaters, and multi-jackpot runs.
Super Streax

Super Streax is a highly sought-after, rare UK pub fruit machine manufactured by Mazooma Games. Running on the popular Scorpion 4 (SC4) hardware platform, it typically featured classic pub stakes such as a £25 jackpot.
Super Street Fighter II Turbo

Super Street Fighter II Turbo is a single-player and two-player versus fighting game. The game continues the international martial arts tournament structure of Street Fighter II, with fighters from around the world competing for their own reasons. Each character has a brief personal motivation and ending, but the main structure centers on one-on-one battles against the rest of the roster. In single-player mode, the selected fighter faces a sequence of computer-controlled opponents before reaching the final battles, while two-player mode allows two human players to fight directly.

The main roster consists of the sixteen fighters from Super Street Fighter II. Returning characters include the original World Warriors, the four boss characters, and the four fighters introduced in the previous version: Cammy, Dee Jay, Fei Long, and T. Hawk. The game also introduces Akuma, known as Gouki in Japan, as a hidden opponent and secret playable character.
Super Street Fighter II Turbo: New Legacy

New Legacy is a Super Street Fighter 2 Turbo hack-rom by Born2SPD.
Balance, variety, bug fixing and new features are the ordered objectives.
New Legacy is still in beta, currently on the v0.7.
Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers

Four new characters, Cammy, Fei Long, Dee Jay, and T. Hawk, have been added to the previous list of characters from this series. Also, the graphics and sound have been improved over the earlier versions.

Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers is the fourth game in the Street Fighter II sub-series of Street Fighter games, following Street Fighter II: Hyper Fighting. In addition to refining and balancing the existing character roster from the previous installments, Super Street Fighter II also introduced four new characters. It was also the first game to be developed on Capcom '​s CP System II hardware, which permitted more sophisticated graphics and audio over the original CP System hardware, used by the previous versions of Street Fighter II.
Super Street Fighter II: The Tournament Battle

This is a special edition of Super Street Fighter II that was designed for eight player tournament matches.

The core gameplay remains the same as the original game, with the main difference being that once matches finish, the winners (and losers) would move to another cabinet to fight against other players in the bracket, until all matches were completed and all players were placed in the match ranking.

The game features specialized graphics and audio that are unique to this edition, used in the attract mode, between matches, and when someone wins a tournament.

If four machines were not linked together, they could still be used as a standard Super Street Fighter II cabinet.
Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition

An arcade version of Super Street Fighter IV was released by Capcom in December 2010, titled Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition. Arcade Edition added Yun, Yang, Evil Ryu and Oni to the roster, as well as changes to the existing characters.
Super Strike

Using a cue ball, you roll the ball into the machine. An IR sensor reads where the ball rolls, and knocks down pins accordingly. There are variations of bowling including regular bowling, Strike or Die and Flash.
Super Strong Warriors
Super Strong Warriors is a boxing arcade game developed by Jaleco in 1993. It's the first title of the Jaleco Mega System 32.
Super Stud

Super Stud is a card game released by Mirco in 1977.

Super Stud captures all the fun, excitement & suspense of a traditional favorite... five card stud poker.
Super Surfin'

The Super Surfin' fruit machine is a classic UK slot machine manufactured by Gemini (a brand tightly associated with or under Barcrest).
The machine was built on Barcrest's iconic MPU4 hardware platform, which was the industry standard for pub and arcade fruit machines across the UK during the late 1980s and 1990s.
Super Tank

Super Tank is one of two original games manufactured by German company Video Games GmbH. Released in 1981, it was licensed to SNK for the Japanese market and Computran for the US Market.

In Super Tank, up to two players simultaneously control highly mobile armored tanks on a mission to destroy the SUPER TANK. An introductory collection round challenges the players to clear a field of mines and destroy as many red enemy tanks as possible. Special glowing diamonds are scattered throughout, providing temporary super armor protection and making the players’ task easier.

After clearing the field of mines, the players are ready for their confrontation with the SUPER TANK! The SUPER TANK is this game’s most dangerous adversary. It is a highly-maneuverable vehicle with a single weakness at the tip of its nozzle. A direct hit on the nozzle will destroy the SUPER TANK, bringing the players to another more intricate collection round where the challenges are greater and so are the rewards.
Super Tank Attack

Super Tank Attack is a prototype 3D vehicle combat game developed by MicroProse for arcade where the player pilots a futuristic battle tank through open arenas filled with enemy vehicles, missile turrets, and destructible structures. 

The game is presented in a first-person cockpit view, displaying radar, damage indicators, and ammunition readouts. Using a joystick and throttle setup, the player moves the tank across the battlefield, locking on and firing at enemy armor units. Each arena contains multiple opposing tanks and obstacles such as towers and fuel tanks that can be destroyed for extra points.

The goal is to eliminate as many enemies as possible before the arena timer expires. Power-ups and secondary weapons, such as guided missiles or high-powered shells, increase firepower but are limited in supply. Two players can participate simultaneously in linked arenas or split-screen setups, competing for score or survival.
Super Tarzan

The Super Tarzan fruit machine is an arcade slot game developed by the Taiwanese manufacturer International Game System (IGS). Originally released in the late 1990s or early 2000, this game functions as a classic "Cherry Master" style video slot board.
Super Thunder Blade

This follow-up to Thunder Blade is very similar to the original arcade game. Get into a helicopter and blast away at the numerous enemies with its cannon and missiles. The game's four stages all follow a similar pattern: the first part is from a perspective behind the helicopter where players not only have to dodge enemy fire but also obstacles like buildings or caves. In between, players face off against one or two smaller boss enemies. When the first part of a level is finished, the view switches to an overhead perspective for the confrontation with the level's end boss.
Super Toffy

Super Toffy is an improved version of Toffy, which in turn is a bootleg of the game Dangerous Dungeons with updated sprites. Super Toffy revamps many levels, getting rid of the recycled levels found in Dangerous Dungeons that are the same as other levels with minor changes or just upping the treasure requirement. 

Super Toffy adds an item that freezes the enemies in place temporarily - though even when they're frozen, you still can't stand next to the goombas (which replace spiders in DD) or the green faces (which replace octopi in DD). Super Toffy also adds artwork between stages.

Finally, unlike DD, there are a couple of score-based extends; you can get up to 5 lives.
Super Treasure Island
Super Treasure Island: 3 X 3 video bingo gambling game with 8 pay lines featuring 256 colour graphics, sounds and double up feature.
Super Trio

Super Trio is a side-scrolling platform shoot-em-up arcade game released in 1994 by the South Korean developer Game Ace (also published on MS-DOS by Dong Sung Joycom in 1995). It features a cutesy, Super Mario Bros.-style aesthetic but mixes it with running and shooting gameplay.
Super Triv-Quiz

Super Triv Quiz was produced by Status in 1986.

A trivia game from Status.
Super Trivia Master

Super Trivia Master is a one to four player quiz game published and developed by Enerdyne Technologies in 1986.

The sequel to The 1985 Trivia Master quiz game.
Super Twenty One
Super Twenty One is a video blackjack game for up to four players. It was developed by Micro Games in 1978. It is an update to their original 21 game that they released two years prior.
Super Visual Soccer: Sega Cup

Super Visual Soccer, known as Super Visual Football in Europe and The J. League 1994 in Japan (in which it has a license to use teams from the Japanese J. League), is a football game for Sega System 32 arcade hardware.
Super Volley Ball

Indoor competitive volleyball game where the U.S. can battle Cuba, Japan, China, and U.S.S.R. Player controls bumping, spiking, blocking, and serving. Killer spikes are rewarded with a cry of "Nice spike!", a cheering crowd, and a goofy picture of the spiking player.
Super Wing
Super Wing is a computerized arcade pinball game for 1-2 players (alternating turns) developed and released by Wing in 1985.
Super World Court

Super World Court is a tennis game and sequel to World Court. There are sixteen players to choose from: seven male, six female, as well as one robot, cat and frog. The game includes four tournaments - American Open (hard court), French Open (clay), British Open (grass) and Namco Open which features a cameo appearance by Namco's mascot Pac-Man. Singles and doubles matches (supporting up to 4 players simultaneously) are available.
Super World Stadium

Super World Stadium (スーパーワールドスタジアム, literally: Sūpā Wārudo Sutajiamu), is a baseball arcade game that was released by Namco in 1991, exclusively in Japan. It runs on Namco System 2 hardware and is the fourth title in the company's World Stadium series; much like its predecessors, it used a Yamaha YM-2151 FM sound chip (for all its songs this time as opposed to just the secondary ones), but it used a C140 custom sound chip for its sound effects and speech (as opposed to a PSG and DAC). It also features: sixteen teams (as opposed to only twelve - ten of the teams are returning favorites from the three System 1-era titles, but six of them were created specifically for this game).
Super World Stadium '92

Super World Stadium '92 Gekitouban (スーパーワールドスタジアム'92激闘版, literally: Sūpā Wārudo Sutajiamu '92 Gekitōban) is a baseball arcade game that was released by Namco in 1992 exclusively in Japan. It runs on Namco System 2 hardware, and is the sixth title in the company's World Stadium series.

Super World Stadium '92 Gekitouban's gameplay is identical to Super World Stadium '92. The game is different in that it has three extra Kanji characters on its title screen, adding "Gekitouban." This difference illustrates the fact that it has a brand-new "FAVOR" setting in its options menu (which is set to "NONE" by default, but could be set to any one of the twelve new-for-1992 teams in order to make the game display any one of the twelve screens shown below during its attract sequence).
Super World Stadium '93

Super World Stadium '93 , is a baseball arcade game that was released by Namco in 1993 exclusively in Japan. It runs on Namco System 2 hardware, and is the seventh (and last NS2-era) title in the company's World Stadium series; like its predecessors, it used a Yamaha YM-2151 FM sound chip (for all its songs this time, as opposed to just the secondary ones) - but it used a C140 custom sound chip for its sound effects and speech (as opposed to a PSG and DAC). The Yokohama Taiyo Whales have also undergone a renaming, to "Yokohama Baystars".
Super World Stadium '95

Super World Stadium '95 (スーパーワールドスタジアム'95, literally Sūpā Wārudo Sutajiamu '95), is a baseball arcade game that was released by Namco in 1995, only in Japan. It runs upon Namco NB-1 hardware and is the eighth title in the company's World Stadium series; it was also the first title in the series that did not use a Yamaha YM-2151 FM sound chip for music (instead, it used a C352 custom sound chip for everything), and features the same twelve real-life teams from the three previous titles (including the Yokohama Baystars, who were known as the "Yokohama Taiyo Whales" up until 1993).
Super World Stadium '96

Super World Stadium '96 (スーパーワールドスタジアム'96, literally Sūpā Wārudo Sutajiamu '96), is a baseball arcade game that was released by Namco in 1996, only in Japan. It runs upon Namco NB-1 hardware and is the ninth title in the company's World Stadium series; it is also the second title in the series that did not use a Yamaha YM-2151 FM sound chip for music (instead, it used a C352 custom sound chip for everything) and features the twelve real teams from the four previous titles (as well as the fictional Sixties, Seventies, Eighties, Nineties and USA that were created specifically for this one).
Super World Stadium '97

Super World Stadium '97 (スーパーワールドスタジアム'97, literally Sūpā Wārudo Sutajiamu '97), is a baseball arcade game that was released by Namco in 1997, only in Japan. It runs upon Namco NB-1 hardware, and is the tenth title in the company's World Stadium series; it was also the third title in the series that did not use a Yamaha YM-2151 FM sound chip for music (instead, it used a C352 custom sound chip for everything), and features the twelve real teams from the five previous titles (as well as the fictional team of the "USA" created specifically for Super World Stadium '96 in the previous year).
Super World Stadium '98
Super World Stadium '98 is a Sports game, developed and published by Namco, which was released in Japan in 1998.
Super World Stadium '99

Super World Stadium '99 (スーパーワールドスタジアム'99, literally Sūpā Wārudo Sutajiamu '99), is a baseball arcade game that was released by Namco in 1999, only in Japan. It runs on Namco System 12 hardware and is the eleventh (and final) title in the company's long-running World Stadium series; it is also the last title in the series that does not use a Yamaha YM-2151 FM sound chip for music (as with its three NB-1-era predecessors, it uses a C352 custom sound chip for everything), and the only title in the series to feature three-dimensional polygonal graphics (with non-identical-looking players).
Super World Stadium 2000

Super World Stadium 2000 was produced by Namco in 2000.

A one or two player sports game
Super World Stadium 2001
Super World Stadium 2001 is a Sports game, developed and published by Namco, which was released in Japan in 2001.
Super Xevious

Super Xevious was produced by Namco in 1984.

The player controls a fighter with guns and bombs that must infiltrate a highly defended area and destroy everything in sight. The overall goal is to destroy the motherships that pop up periodically.

Super Xevious takes place on Earth. An invading alien race has set up shop, and it's up to the player to send 'em home. The game has a large number of different ground and air-based targets of either belligerent or non-belliegerent nature. In addition to the jumper-based difficulty levels, the game also adapts its difficulty to the player. If the player is successful against a type of attacker, an even deadlier type of attacker shows up to challenge the player.

The game play is very much like the original Xevious, but in this sequel, the play is a little more difficult. Several new enemies are introduced, including a silver Galaxian flagship, two jet planes, a helicopter, and a dark yellow tank.
Super Xevious: GAMP no Nazo

Once again, inhabitants from the planet Xevious, controlled by the super-computer GAMP, are attacking the Earth, their ancient home planet, willing to re-capture it by force. The SOL towers have emerged from the ground on our planet, remotely controlled by GAMP, aiding the Xevians in their invasion. Only the brave pilots of the Solvalou aircraft are able to avert this new threat!

Super Xevious is a 2D vertically-scrolling shoot 'em up. Power-ups such as bombs, lasers, and shields can be collected; the latter protects the aircraft from immediate destruction if hit by an enemy. Other power-ups for the Solvalou include a rear shot and a bigger lock-on. Some stages are completed by fulfilling certain requirements, rather than simply proceeding, eliminating all enemies; if these are not met, the stage will loop indefinitely, sending progressively harder enemies.
Super Zaxxon

Super Zaxxon is a three-quarter perspective, space shooter style game. You must first go over a base on an asteroid. Things located on this base include gun implacements, fuel tanks, radar stations, missiles, and fighters. After you successfully navigate this base, you will go through a tunnel to tangle with enemy fighters, mine layers, and mines. You then will have to navigate through a series of barriers on another asteroid in order to take on the Super Zaxxons, the enemy robot dragons.

The game is very similar in appearance to Zaxxon. The differences are:

- Your fighter moves much faster. This makes going after ground targets a big challenge.

- The graphics are different. Although this is more of a viewing difference, it can still change ones perspective after they have gotten used to the Zaxxon graphics.

- There is no more outer space battle. Instead, you must go through a narrow tunnel to get to area 3.
Super-X

Super X was developed by Korean manufacturer Dooyong and published by Mitchell in 1994

A space shooter from Korean company Dooyong and published by Mitchell.
Superbike

Superbike is an action game developed in 1983 by Century Electronics. 

It is essentially a shooting game that masquerades itself as a stunt bike game in which you have to jump over objects like trees, holes, and buses in order to rack up points. Plays somewhat like Moon Patrol.
Superior Soldiers

August 1999. 90% of humanity has died due to a strange energy falling on Earth. The remaining humans have named this energy Force. To protect themselves against the Force they have remodeled their bodies and created a new generation of man.

Besides the names of several characters, the North American version, Superior Soldiers lacks other things that are seen in the Japanese version, Perfect Soldiers. The Japanese version has an announcer shouting the name of the game at the title screen, as well as names of "who VS. who" at the VS. screens in Engrish. However, the well-known "Winners Don't Use Drugs" screen and new color graphics were added to the North American version.
Superman

Clark Kent, a mild-mannered reporter for a great metropolitan newspaper, possesses a secret - when he pulls off his coat, he becomes Superman, a strange being from another planet with powers and abilities far beyond those of mortal men. Our hero will need those powers and abilities, because Earth is under attack again! Time for Superman to take some serious action.

Superman is basically an alternative multi-scrolling beat'em up and multi-scrolling shoot'em up. Some of the stages are set on ground level where Superman can walk or fly at a low attitude and some find Superman flying high as the action changes to a shoot'em up.
Sure Shot Pool

Sure Shot Pool was produced by Status in 1988.

A billiards game from Status.
Surf Planet

Surf Planet is a 3D arcade snowboarding game played using a behind view. It uses a standing cabinet system with a single joystick for control. Optionally two cabinets can be linked for competitive play. There are four riders to choose from as well as four courses with an increasing difficulty: Mt. Cook, Mt. Blanc, Mt. Mc Kinley and Lake Tahoe. The races are done starting with a helicopter drop against three opponents and it is possible to hinder each other. The game uses a rock soundtrack.

While riding there is a time limit and checkpoints need to be reached soon enough to extend the time and continue the race. The game encourages doing stunts and looking for shortcuts. Optimal speed can be achieved by collecting snowboard wax. This fills a meter in the top right corner, ranging from bad to perfect, which influences the maximum speed.
Surprise Attack

Surprise Attack is 2D platform game, little similar to Rolling Thunder or Shinobi. The player must neutralize terrorists, who take base on mars, and defuse time bombs. Gameplay is quite simple - hero goes right, shoots enemies, finds bombs, avoid enemy bullets etc, he must jump on upper floors to bypass obstacles (and neutralize some bombs).
Survival

Survival was produced by Rock-Ola Mfg. Corp. in 1982.

A maze game where the player controls a large blue cell that zaps medicine into the veins. Each vein that is zapped will disappear from the maze. A
Survival Arts

The birthplace of the powerful physical martial arts called "Survival Arts" and how they were earned became mysterious for quite some time. However, eight warriors spreading over different countries have learned some of the most important skills of the Survival Arts, while they continue learning more about them. Each one qualified for the Survival Arts tournament to see which survivor will win and obtain all the secrets of the Arts.
Sushi Bar

Sushi Bar is a puzzle game for the Sammy Atomiswave arcade board. The gameplay is very similar with Puyo Puyo where the player must rearrange various foods of the traditional Japanese culinary to unlock the next level. The game was released only in Japan.
Susume! Taisen Puzzle-Dama

Taisen Puzzle-Dama (対戦ぱずるだま, lit. "Battle Puzzle Ball") is a puzzle series developed by Konami.

The gameplay of the series is similar to other matching-based puzzle games, such as Puyo Puyo, being a battle game between one player and either a human or CPU opponent. Balls will descend down the screen, in colours red, yellow, blue, or green. These balls can be either "large balls" (おおだま, Ōdama) or "small balls" (こだま, Kodama), the latter of which appear "locked" in square boxes. Large balls are cleared if three or more are touching horizontally or vertically. When a large ball is cleared next to a small ball, that small ball is "unlocked" and becomes a large ball, and so can be matched with. If a combo of matches occurs, those balls are converted into "attack balls" (こうげきだま, Kougeki dama), which results in small balls being added to the opponent's side, in a different pattern for each character.

The ball types are as follows:

Large Ball (おおだま, Ōdama): Basic ball type, can be matched.
Suzuka 8 Hours

Suzuka 8 Hours is an arcade game based on the famous 8 hour endurance motorbike race held on the Suzuka Circuit in Japan. Instead of racing for the full 8 hours you have to try to complete four laps against the clock on your own or against a friend. As the race is against the clock the other riders on the track are just there to overtake without crashing. Hitting another rider or an obstacle on the side of the track throws you off your bike and wastes precious seconds. The longer the race goes on the game slowly changes from racing in the day to racing at night.

Suzuka 8 Hours is viewed from a 3rd person perspective and you and a friend sit on replicas of bikes using handlebars to steer, accelerate and brake your bike.
Suzuka 8 Hours 2

Suzuka 8 Hours 2 (鈴鹿8アワーズ2, Eng. Suzuka Ēto Awāzu Tsū), is a racing arcade game that was released by Namco in 1993, only in Japan; it runs upon Namco System 2 hardware, and as the name suggests, it is the sequel to Suzuka 8 Hours, which was released in the previous year. The gameplay is much the same as that of the original, except that this time there are four different tracks to choose from - the original Suzuka Circuit (making its fifth appearance in a Namco racing game after PP2, FL, FL2 and the original S8H), the "Green Hill Circuit" (which despite its name, does not take place in the initial Zone for Sonic the Hedgehog), the "Bayside Raceway", and finally the "Devil's Canyon Circuit".

That Green Hill Circuit is the easiest of the four tracks (and is recommended for novice players); once you have mastered it, you will be ready to move on to the Bay Side Raceway (which is the equivalent of the Monacan and San Marinan tracks from FL2 and 3).
SWAT

In this arcade title, the player controls SWAT, a shooting hoverboarder. The game appears to be set underwater, and each stage is almost a fixed background - though there is a tiny bit of up-and-down scrolling.

Aliens resembling sea creatures try to build a tunnel from the bottom of the stage to the top, which is your home-base.

If you touch an alien you die, and if an alien builds a tunnel right up to your home-base it gains control of it and shoots jets of fire down at you.

Besides shooting a rapid-fire laser gun, you can fire torpedoes which attach to tunnel sections and explode on a timer, allowing you to get out of range. You die if caught in the blast. Besides being able to destroy tunnel sections with your missile weapons, you can also shove them to the side.
SWAT Police

Swat Police is a single player shooting gallery video game for Arcade, created and published by ESD in 2001.

A gun shooting, horizontal scroll action game that uses joysticks and buttons rather than guns. One player can play on their own, or 2 players can team up and play simultaneously as the two SWAT police characters, Cruise and James.
Sweet Gal

Sweet Gal is a classic coin-operated arcade video game produced by the Japanese company Nichibutsu (Nihon Bussan Co. Ltd.) and released in 1986.

Developed and published by Nichibutsu, a prominent Japanese arcade developer known for its extensive catalogue of mahjong, sci-fi, and adult-themed arcade games.
Sweet Hearts II
Sweet Hearts II is a slot machine game developed and published by Aristocrat in 1998.
Sweet Life 2

Sweet Life 2 is a classic video slot machine developed by the well-known software provider Igrosoft and released in 2009. The game features a comical Siberian grizzly bear on a quest to steal honey from a bee garden.
Swimmer

Swimmer is a action game in which the player has to swim up a river avoiding obstacles by either dodging them or diving under them while picking up fruit along the way for score. A bonus score is awarded at the end of level based on the fruit you collected. Obstacles come in the form of logs and other swimming critters.

At the end of each level, there is a giant crab that has to be avoided to go to the next level. At later levels you can pick up power pills that allow you to eat the marine life. The objective is to reach the island in the stream and once that is achieved the levels repeat.
Swingin In The Green

"Swingin' in the Green" is a classic multi-line video slot machine released by WMS Gaming in 1999. Operating on the popular WMS 550 cabinet platform, it became a staple of casino floors in the early 2000s and is remembered for its distinctive cartoon art style and interactive bonus mechanics.
Swinging Singles

Swinging Singles is an extremely rare, adult-themed maze arcade game released in 1983 by a company called Entertainment LTD (often listed as Ent., Limited).
The player controls a car moving through a series of grid-based labyrinths.
You must navigate the maze while avoiding hazards, obstacles, and pursuing police officers.
The core mission requires navigating to a specific "orgy house" within the maze to locate a key. Once the key is obtained, it unlocks a door that transitions the player to an explicit pixelated encounter with a prostitute.
Sword Art Online Arcade: Deep Explorer

A mysterious space that suddenly appeared in The Seed's network, commonly known as "Unknown".

You will support Kirito and his friends who are diving into the Unknown from the new game machine "ViSTer" at the game center, and will challenge the adventure together.

Supports not only single-player play, but also in-store/online co-op play for up to 3 people!
Synchronica

Synchronica Arcade Machine is a vibrant touch-screen rhythm game where players can go solo or challenge each other to climb the high score charts!

The name "Synchronica" reflects the core gameplay, which involves tapping and sliding on the touch screen in sync with on-screen prompts. So far, actions include single, double, and triple taps, along with diagonal upward slides.

The game features a variety of music genres, including the ever-popular J-POP. Notably, the VOCALOID trademark appears on the screen, hinting at the inclusion of beloved Vocaloid characters and tracks.

Although it features the familiar characters and art style from Taiko no Tatsujin, Synchronica stands apart with its use of a touch interface instead of the traditional drum-and-stick controls.
Syougi No Tatsujin: Master of Syougi
The 'Syougi' is a Japanese chess-style game.
Syusse Oozumou

Syusse Ōzumō is an arcade game themed on professional sumo wrestling. The player begins as a low-ranked wrestler and advances through tournaments, winning bouts to rise toward the rank of yokozuna.

Each match consists of pushing, throwing, and countering until one wrestler is forced out of the ring or knocked down. As the player progresses, opponents become faster and stronger, and timing becomes increasingly critical.
Syvalion
T-MEK

T-Mek is essentially an updated Battlezone. You are a warrior battling in the T-Mek competition, a hugely popular event in the future. You control a hovercraft and try to blow up everyone else.

The action is viewed from your perspective as you travel around the arena. You also have an overall view of where your opponents are. Terrain surfaces and characteristics vary in each battle. In most levels you need to reach a certain score to progress, however there are out-and-out one-off Deathmatch duels to deal with periodically.
T.N.K III

During the final days of World War II, the allied forces sends special forces member Colonel Ralf to penetrate an enemy base and destroy a secret weapon by driving a new prototype tank.

This was the first appearance of Ralf Jones, protagonist of "Ikari Warriors", and a fighter in "The King of Fighters '94" and its sequels. Unlike Ikari and KOF games, which were set in modern times, T.N.K. III is set during World War II.
T.T Mahjong

T.T Mahjong is a foundational 1981 arcade game developed and released by Taito Corporation exclusively in Japan. It holds an important place in video game history as one of the earliest entries to establish the standard convention for computerised Mahjong gameplay.

The game was not originally built from scratch by Taito; it is a direct, licensed variant of the legendary game Jongputer created by Alpha Denshi (and published by Sanritsu Giken). Due to subsequent trademark issues surrounding the Jongputer name, Taito rebranded their authorized manufactured version to "T.T Mahjong".
T.T. Block

T.T Block was produced by Taito in 1977.

A paddle tries to rebound a ball into the bricks.
T.T. Fitter

T.T. Fitter (often referred to simply as Fitter) is a rare, classic maze arcade game released in 1981 by Taito Corporation. The "T.T." prefix in the title stands for Table Top, denoting Taito's iconic cocktail cabinet format popular during the golden age of arcade gaming, though the game also ran in standard vertical raster cabinets.
The game is technically a clone or alternate version of the game Roundup (developed by Amenip/Centuri).

In T.T. Fitter, you control a white robot navigating a grid-like maze.
Table Tennis Champions
Table Tennis Champions was released in June 1995.
Tac/Scan

Tac/Scan (タック・スキャン) is an arcade shoot-'em up developed by Sega Electronics in 1982. It runs on the vector version of the G80 hardware.

Enemy airships are approaching your command base! You need to fly your five plane squadron into battle to defend it. You control a squadron of five ships at the bottom of the screen, your goal is to earn as many points as possible by destroying the various enemies which will be attacking. If one of the ships in your squadron is hit by enemy fire, it will be destroyed. The game ends when all five ships have been destroyed. As you progress through the game, you will occasionally have the chance to replenish missing ships. Everytime you complete a round by shooting ten enemies, an extra ship will float by on the screen. You can add this ship to your squadron by catching it in an empty space in the formation. Every time you complete four rounds, the game will advance to the next level with increased difficulty!
Tactician

Tactician is a fixed shooter arcade game, which was developed by Konami in 1981 and licensed to Sega for manufacture and distribution; it runs on a modified version of Namco's Pac-Man hardware with the video system used in both Rally-X games, first used by Jungler earlier in 1981 (a Zilog Z80 lead microprocessor running at 3.072 MHz with an added Zilog Z80 sub-microprocessor running at 1.789772 MHz, and two General Instrument AY-3-8910s running at the same speed for audio). The player must use a 4-way joystick to direct a ship around the bottom of the screen (with two buttons, the first for firing shots at the enemies, and the second for making barricades by placing small dots around the playfield at the start of each section before the enemies emerge from their bases) - and after thirty seconds, the enemies will emerge from their bases and begin to attack the player's ship.
Tae Kwon Dough
Tae Kwon Dough is a classic UK pub fruit machine manufactured by QPS Interactive (a subsidiary of the Novomatic Group).
Tag Team Wrestling
A wrestling game that focused on teams. You can either play as a face team (the good guys) or a heel team (the baddies)!
Tahjong Yakitori

Tahjong Yakitori is a classic Japanese Mahjong arcade game released in 1985 by Bally Pond and Nasco.

In Japanese Riichi Mahjong, the term "Yakitori" (literally meaning "grilled chicken") is used to describe a player who fails to win a single hand during an entire match.

The 1985 arcade machine is a digitized adaptation centered around this concept, requiring the player to successfully clear hands to avoid facing the "grilled chicken" penalty.
Taihou de Doboon

Taihou de Doboon is a fixed-screen shooter where players fire a cannon at on-screen characters. Hitting a target knocks it into the sea for a win; if the target escapes to the left or right, the attempt fails. Successful hits pay out medals (arcade tokens purchased from the venue). A two-bet mode adds two medals to every listed payout.
Taiko no Tatsujin
Taiko no Tatsujin Arcade is a rhythm game created by Namco. The first of the Taiko no Tatsujin series, gameplay involves beating a taiko drum in time with music.
Taiko no Tatsujin (2020)

The 2020 release of Taiko no Tatsujin, nicknamed Nijiiro Version is a Taiko no Tatsujin arcade that was released in Japan on March 24, 2020 and in Asia regions in Spring 2021. It supersedes the Green Version.
Taiko No Tatsujin 10

The 10th arcade Taiko, released on July 2007. Another big step for the series, this version was the first one to have secret unlockable songs deep within the arcade software. They are unlocked by hitting the rims of the drum in a certain order after your coins are slotted in. The methods of unlocking secret songs would be placed on Namco's official Taiko blog (which was started together with Taiko 10 and DS1).

Not many other changes were made, except now, instead of 'Game Over', the arcade presents the message in full Japanese (it says 'おしまい　まだあそんだね！-oshimai, mada asonda ne! ' meaning 'The game has ended, come play again soon!') and an option is presented to people who still prefer to see the songs arranged by difficulty- just hit the left and right rims quickly one after the other at the song selection screen to switch orders. Plus, the tutorial is no longer forced onto players selecting Kantan, instead placing an option to open the tutorial right next to Kantan.
Taiko no Tatsujin 11

Several new changes were made into this version, with the Extra Extreme (Japanese: 裏おに, Ura Oni) track finally added for selected songs for more high skilled players.

The new "Helping Hand Mode"[1] (Japanese: パパママサポート, Papa Mama Sapōto, lit Papa Mama Support) was added, allowing help with family members to help with children by allowing both drums to be used by the child, and the family member.

The Revival Roulette was changed to become the Revival Drumroll. Instead of hitting the right spot, You now have to eat as much food as you can to continue playing for another song.

The results screen added a feature where you can see how many Drum roll hits you beaten.

Asian Version
Taiko no Tatsujin 11: Asian Version was the version of Taiko no Tatsujin 11 that was localized to China. It was the first release of Taiko no Tatsujin in the arcades to be localized to Mainland China, as well as Taiwan, and Hong Kong.
Taiko no Tatsujin 11: Asian Version

Taiko no Tatsujin 11: Asian Version is a localized 2008 arcade release designed for Mainland China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong. Developed by Bandai Namco, it features identical gameplay to the Japanese release but includes Chinese voice acting for Don-chan and an exclusive 25-song C-Pop category.
Taiko no Tatsujin 12

The 12th Taiko arcade machine, released in December 2008. Taiko 12 marked a plateau as far as development of the series was concerned- the game mechanics and graphics have been perfected over so many different versions. No major fixes or upgrades were made on this version, except for one small thing- instead of 'Taiko no Tatsujin Twelve' being announced on the title screen, it was replaced with the Japanese equivalent 'Jyuu-ni' (which also means twelve).
Taiko no Tatsujin 12: Asian Version

Taiko no Tatsujin 12: Asian Version is a classic arcade rhythm game originally released by Bandai Namco in 2009. It is known for its physical, simulated taiko drum controller and features over 110 songs across various genres, including J-Pop, Anime, and Namco Originals.

While largely similar to the Japanese release, the Asia version often included a few unique Asian-localized tracks or alternate versions of J-Pop/Anime songs. It includes multiplayer support for up to two players to either cooperate or compete against one another in rhythm battles. The music is broken down into classic categories: Pop, Anime, Variety, Children/Folk, Classical, Game, and Namco Original.
Taiko no Tatsujin 13

The 13th Taiko no Tatsujin, released on December 2009 just five months after the wildly successful Taiko 12.5. Taiko 13 takes the game to new heights, being the first version to be used in a nationwide (Japan, of course) official Taiko no Tatsujin tournament in April 2010. In terms of new features, again it doesn't introduce many new things, except a slight change in the Children/Folk genre name from Kanji to hiragana.

Being the first arcade to introduce alternate methods of unlocking secret songs other than entering secret codes, a few of them were leaked to players long before the official secret code was given out. Even Namco played along by offering players hints along the way. There was a lot of deduction on the exact method to unlock songs without secret codes, but all of them required an expert hand in FCing a song on triple speed or something or other.
Taiko no Tatsujin 14

Taiko no Tatsujin 14 is the fourteen arcade Taiko no Tatsujin game released on September 8, 2010.

Being released in 2010, it is the last Taiko no Tatsujin arcade game which uses the Namco System 246.

There were new changes to the 14th release, If the player got a Full Combo on a song, flowers and a drapery will appear spelling "Full Combo!".

There was also a new type of fever character that would appear when the player has a full gauge, just for Taiko no Tatsujin 14. They also appeared on the Wii U, and the newer arcade versions.

A new scoring system was added called the "Shin-uchi Mode", It can only be unlocked by hitting the edge of the Taiko 10 times once coins are inserted. Shin-uchi Mode calculates score based on accuracy instead of combos. However, when using Shin-uchi Mode, high-scores were not recorded.
Taiko no Tatsujin 2

Taiko no Tatsujin 2 is the second Taiko no Tatsujin arcade game released on August 6, 2001.

The main gameplay mechanics is the same as the first Taiko no Tatsujin arcade.

Unlike the first Taiko no Tatsujin arcade where there's only one difficulty each song, there are now multiple difficulties for each song/music. Taiko no Tatsujin 2 also introduces the Donderful difficulty (updated in Taiko no Tatsujin 7 as the Oni difficulty). All the songs appear in this difficulty. However, the notes are same as the hard level.

Starting from this version, the number of combo hits are shown on the screen, starting from 10 combos.
Taiko no Tatsujin 3

Taiko no Tatsujin 3 is the third Taiko no Tatsujin arcade game released on March 15, 2002.

Along with additional songs, the third arcade release is the first to introduce balloon notes, as well as the battle mode between two players. Instead of having their own Tamashii gauges, both players share one. Hitting the notes will increase the tamashii meter, while missing the notes will cause the tamashii meter to reduce. The player who has the longer tamashii meter at the end of the song wins.

Starting from this version, an icon of the difficulty level is shown on the gameplay screen.
Taiko no Tatsujin 4
Taiko no Tatsujin 4 is the 4th installment of the Taiko no Tatsujin series released for arcade on December 12, 2002.
Taiko no Tatsujin 5

Taiko no Tatsujin 5 is the fifth arcade Taiko no Tatsujin game released on October 6, 2003.

There was a new mode for the Song Select in Taiko no Tatsujin 5. The player can now choose a song first before making a difficulty selection. However, the player cannot choose "Donderful!" in the song select mode.
Taiko no Tatsujin 6

Taiko no Tatsujin 6 is the sixth arcade Taiko no Tatsujin game released on July 15, 2004.

Being released 7 days before Atsumare! Matsuri da!! Yondaime, it was the last Taiko no Tatsujin arcade game with the 1st generation graphics, plus being the last version to have the "Donderful!" difficulty as the 4th difficulty's name, as it was renamed to Oni in Taiko no Tatsujin 7.

Taiko no Tatsujin 6 added a feature where the player can choose the same song more than once per play, but only if the song is chosen before difficulty.
Taiko No Tatsujin 7

Taiko no Tatsujin 7 is the first second-generation Taiko no Tatsujin arcade game, which runs on the Namco System 246 that has similar specs to that of the PlayStation 2. As such, the graphics were overhauled.

Unlike previous releases, all songs now can be played on all difficulties. The Highest difficulty, the Donderful difficulty, has been renamed as Oni. The name of said difficulty in English was stayed as such until the release of Taiko no Tatsujin: Drum Session!.

Staring with this game, the song categories were overhauled, and stayed as such (with new song category additions over time) until the release of Taiko no Tatsujin (2020).

The Yam notes, invisible modifier and the Go-Go Time system, which were first introduced in Taiko no Tatsujin: Go! Go! Godaime, was implemented into the arcade platform for the first time.
Taiko No Tatsujin 8

Taiko no Tatsujin 8 is the eighth arcade Taiko no Tatsujin game released on March 23, 2006.

Although the core gameplay is mostly unchanged, there are numerous changes that were made to Taiko no Tatsujin 8.

The double, triple, and quadruple speed settings, and the Game Music category from Taiko no Tatsujin: Wai Wai Happy! Rokudaime were added.

Also new to this release is the new Revival Roulette. If the Donder fail to clear the first song, they will have to play a roulette, and if they hit the right spot during a roulette, they get to continue playing until they either finished all the song queues or failed to Norma-cleared 2nd to 4th songs.
Taiko No Tatsujin 9

Taiko no Tatsujin 9 is the ninth entry of Taiko no Tatsujin arcade game released in December 20, 2006.

The graphic interfaces for the song select, and gameplay had been changed to match Taiko no Tatsujin Doka! to Oomori Nanadaime's new interface that was released along with it.
Taiko no Tatsujin RT: Nippon no Kokoro

Taiko no Tatsujin RT: Nihon no Kokoro is an arcade designed specifically for the elderly and disabled people. It was released in November 2004 and contains 20 songs.

This game was designed as a form of physiotherapy for the disabled and elderly. As such, it has lower drum placements for accessibility, and only Easy and Normal as the available difficulties.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Blue Version

Taiko no Tatsujin: Blue Version is a Taiko no Tatsujin arcade that was released on March 25, 2018. It supersedes the Yellow Version.

It was superseded by Green Version on March 14, 2019.

Blue Version carried over most of the gameplay modes and function from the previous arcade version, as such, core gameplay is identical. The practice mode, which was introduced in previous version, was removed from Blue Version.

New to this update is the addition of the Performance Battle Mode that was added on June 27, 2018; It has similar gameplay as the battle mode in the recently released Taiko no Tatsujin games on Nintendo DS and 3DS.

Story:
In a fantasy world, there is a crisis where a giant black dragon have turns humans into vicious monsters. Those very monsters will only revert to be human once they were defeated with the rhythm power.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Green Version

Taiko no Tatsujin: Green Version is a Taiko no Tatsujin arcade that was released on March 14, 2019. It supersedes the Blue Version.

It was superseded by Nijiiro Version on March 24, 2020.

Green version carried over most of the gameplay modes and function from the previous arcade version, as such, core gameplay is identical.

The performance battle mode from the Blue Version was removed from the arcade's launch, and is replaced by the AI Battle Performance mode that put donder to play against AI Don who mimics donder's taiko drum skill.

Unlike performance battle mode which is health-based, AI Battle Performance mode determine result by score, combo, combo timing and number of drumrolls. During a songplay, a song's notechart was split into 5 segments. As AI Don will always mimic donder's more recent skill, AI Don will become harder to beat as donder is getting more experienced.

The one who have better scores in 3 of 5 segments or more wins.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Kimidori Version

This is the Asian equivalent of Taiko no Tatsujin Kimidori, released in Japan on July 2014 and in Asia just one month later. Due to licensing problems, the songlist is significantly smaller than its Japanese counterpart, however some progress has been made as all the licensed songs that were released on JP Kimidori on Day 1 are present in this version. Non-promotional event extra folders are also added to this build, in line with JP Kimidori.

Feature-wise there is not much change or major upgrade from Momoiro; Donder Hiroba and all its associated features such as DonChare and the Ranking Dojo are still absent. Due to how Rewards Shop costumes were handled in Momoiro, Don Points could not be reset for Kimidori, instead the rewards for Kimidori were placed after the final one for Momoiro, unlike the JP equivalent where the points are reset.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Momoiro Version
Released In 2013 replacing the Sorario Version. It was replaced with Kimidori Version in 2014.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Murasaki Version

Taiko no Tatsujin: Murasaki Version is a Taiko no Tatsujin arcade released on March 11, 2015. It superseded the Kimidori Version and most songs are carried over to the new version.

It was superseded by White Version on December 10, 2015.

Most of the features from the previous arcade version, such as Dojo Ranking, Reward Shop and Don Challenge, are carried over from Kimidori Version. Uses of Banapassport is also retained in this version.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Red Version

Taiko no Tatsujin: Red Version is a Taiko no Tatsujin arcade that was released on July 14, 2016. It supersedes the White Version.

It was superseded by Yellow Version on March 15, 2017.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Sorairo Version

Taiko no Tatsujin Sorairo Version, released on March 2013, is the second major update to the two-year-old Taiko HD cabinet without any other hardware revisions, and just like the July 2012 revision (Katsu-Don), all the songs and gameplay features that were gradually added are carried forward to this upgrade, including DonChare, the Dojo Ranking mode and all the song folder options. The name 'Sorairo' is added to the official title logo instead of being a mere codename like Katsu-Don, and the interface gets a fresh blue color in contrast to the warm tones used in the previous firmwares.

Not many new features are introduced in this installment, however the biggest shuffle in the songlist is the relocation of all Vocaloid songs in all genres to their own designated Vocaloid genre, a move which promotes even more proliferation of the voice synthesizers in Taiko. All online player data is also moved from 0.5 to Sorairo without a hitch.
Taiko No Tatsujin: Wadaiko Master Version

Wadaiko Master is the Brazilian version of the Taiko no Tatsujin: Momoiro Version arcade cabinet that was released in 2014.

Due to copyright reasons, only about 30 songs are available there. Also, it does not support the Banapassport card reader.
Taiko no Tatsujin: White Version

Taiko no Tatsujin: White Version is a Taiko no Tatsujin arcade that was released on December 10, 2015. It supersedes the Murasaki Version.

It was superseded by Red Version on July 14, 2016.

Most of the features from the previous arcade version, such as Dojo Ranking (originally removed but re-added in version 3.10 update for the Japanese version and version 3.02 update for the Asian version), Reward Shop and Don Challenge, are carried over from Murasaki Version. Uses of Banapassport is also retained in this version.

However, the Taiko Cram School feature was removed from the last version. In version 9.10 update for the Japanese version, a new mode, known as Practice Mode, was added to the arcade.
Taiko no Tatsujin: Yellow Version

Taiko no Tatsujin: Yellow Version is a Taiko no Tatsujin arcade that was released on March 15, 2017. It supersedes the Red Version.

It was superseded by the Blue Version on March 15, 2018.

The core gameplay of the new arcade is mostly the same as the previous version, with some key differences.

The Don point currency, which was introduced since earlier third-generation Taiko no Tatsujin arcade, has been abolished in this version. Instead, a new in-game currency, known as Don Medals, supersedes the Don points. Much like Don points, players with a Banapassport can earn Don medals by playing the songs. (Except in Dojo Ranking and Tokkun Mode) Unlike Don points however, player will only earns the Don medals in an unchangeable set amount. Don medal earning boost may happen during specific holidays and some promotions.

The in-game reward shop has also changed, in which the shop's contents will be swapped after each change of season.
Tail to Nose

Tail to Nose: Great Championship is a top-down F! racing game where the track rotates around the car. Players choose from six F1 cars and one of two drivers to race on various tracks.

Before racing, players select a circuit, with options like Silverstone, Suzuka, and Monaco. The game requires qualifying laps, with the goal of finishing in the top six to advance. The gameplay emphasizes strategic braking, cornering, and avoiding collisions with other cars. Crashing or running out of time ends the game.

Success is measured by completing races within a time limit and avoiding obstacles such as slower drivers and off-track areas. Players must finish in the top three to see a podium celebration and win the game.
TailGunner

Tail Gunner is a monochrome vector arcade game created by Vectorbeam and released by Cinematronics in 1979. The premise of the game is that the player is the tailgunner of a large space ship. Enemy spacecraft attack the vessel in groups of three, and the player must aim a set of crosshairs and shoot the enemies before they slip past the player's cannons. Because of the game's depicted viewpoint, instead of appearing to fly into the starfield, the stars move toward the center of the screen.

In addition to shooting down the enemy ships, the player is also given limited use of a shield that can block ships from passing. The game ends when ten ships slip past the player's cannon. The game was sold as Tail Gunner II in a sit down cabinet, and its controls consisted of a single metal joystick with fire button integrated to the tip.

Tail Gunner's sound card was more complicated than any Cinemaware/Vectorbeam game before it.
Taisen Hot Gimmick

Taisen Hot Gimmick is a popular series of adult-themed, strip mahjong video games developed and published by Psikyo. Originally debuting in Japanese arcades in 1997, the series sets classic tile-matching mahjong gameplay against diverse anime opponents like students, nurses, and models. Winning rounds depletes the opponent's chips and rewards the player by unlocking distinct visual animations and graphics.
Taisen Hot Gimmick 3 Digital Surfing

Taisen Hot Gimmick 3: Digital Surfing is a mature-themed, "strip mahjong" arcade video game developed and published by Psikyo in August 1999. It is the third entry in Psikyo's infamous Taisen Hot Gimmick series and stands out for its uniquely meta concept: an arcade machine that mimics playing a mahjong game on a Windows PC web browser.

The game was the first in the series to split the experience into three distinct gameplay modes:
1. Digital Surfing (1-Player): The core attraction where players browse a fictional "internet" to play mahjong against 10 distinct opponents (plus one hidden final boss). Defeating opponents triggers the series' hallmark "punishment scenes" where players mash buttons to reveal adult content.
2. Mahjong Fighters (1-Player): A single-player story mode focused entirely on mahjong progression.
3. Jan-Prince vs. Jan-Shogun (2-Player): A competitive split-screen or head-to-head mode for two local players.
Taisen Hot Gimmick 4 Ever

Taisen Hot Gimmick 4 Ever is an adult-themed, competitive mahjong arcade game developed and published by Psikyo. Released in Japan in May 2000, it represents the fourth main installment in the popular Taisen Hot Gimmick franchise.

Players engage in standard Japanese mahjong matches against a lineup of female opponents.
True to the franchise, winning matches triggers interactive sequences. However, 4 Ever famously added options to inflict no punishment on the opponents, showing them happy without forced nudity.
Taisen Hot Gimmick Kairakuten

Taisen Hot Gimmick Kairakuten is a strip mahjong game featuring beautiful graphics and twelve lovely opponents.

After winning three rounds against an opponent or depleting all of her funds, the player is given the choice to 'punish' the opponent. Each girl features two punishment scenes, of which the player may only choose one to view. When shown, the player must repeatedly press the A button to advance the animated sequence to reveal further nudity.

After defeating an opponent (or after a continue) the player may buy cheat items to use against the next opponent.

The game is over once all of the player's betting funds are depleted.
Taisen Hot Gimmick Mix Party
A tabletop mahjong gambling game developed and manufactured by Xnauts in 2005.
Taisen Idol-Mahjong Final Romance 2

Idol Mahjong Final Romance 2 is a strip-mahjong game released in 1995 for the Neo Geo CD in Japan only. It is second title on Video System's Idol Mahjong Final Romance series, ditching the photorealistic pictures from the first title in favor of a anime style for the girls which was kept for the remainder of the series.

Overview
Idol Mahjong Final Romance 2 is a simple mahjong simulator where the player must face off against the various women characters in mahjong matches. Once a girl is defeated the player earns a picture of the girl undressing and moves on to the next match. Points earned during matches can be used to purchase various items between matches which can be used to give the player various advantages during gameplay.
Taisen Mahjong Final Romance 4

Taisen Mahjong Final Romance 4 (対戦麻雀ファイナルロマンス4) is an adult-themed ("strip mahjong") arcade game developed and released by Video System in April 1998. It is the fourth entry in the popular Final Romance idol-mahjong series, following its predecessor, Taisen Mahjong Final Romance R.
Taisen Mahjong Final Romance R

Taisen Mahjong Final Romance R was produced by Video System Co. Ltd. in 1995.

The third Final Romance game. Challenge several girls to strip mahjong. If you win, you get to watch animated strip sequences. Points earned may be spent on cheating devices.
Taisen Tanto-R Sashissu!!

Taisen Tanto-R 'Sasshissu!' was produced by Sega in 1996.

A curious game where you can play a bunch of mini games.
Taisen Tokkae-Dama

Taisen Tokkae Dama (対戦とっかえだま), is a puzzle game developed and published by Konami and released for Arcade platforms on 1996 in Japan. It is part of the Taisen Puzzle-Dama series, and a spin-off of this series.

Taisen Tokkaedama is a 2D puzzle game, somewhat similar to Magical Drop - in that the player must combine balls of the same color. Here, balls rise from the bottom of the screen. The player can grab one and put it in another place. if there are 3 or more balls of the same color - they disappear, and the opponent's screen gets a few more.
Taito Cup Finals

Taito Cup Finals was produced by Taito Japan in 1992.

Football soccer game where you can kick opponents as well as score goals. This is like an old version of the modern day FIFA streets it gives you a hint of were EA got the idea from
Taiwan Chess Legend

Taiwan Chess Legend is a rare, retro arcade game released in 1996.

It digitizes traditional Chinese Chess rules, which may include the standard full-board variant or "Dark Chess" (Anqi), a highly popular Taiwanese casual variant where pieces are turned face-down and flipped over dynamically during play.
Take 5

Five game in one:
 -- Wipe Out (single-player)
 -- Wipe Out (two- or four-player)
 -- Match (two- or four-player)
 -- Pro Match (two-player)
 -- Gravity Match (two- or four-player)
Take The Piece

"Take The Piece" is a classic UK pub fruit machine manufactured by Bell-Fruit Games (BFG). Originally released in the late 1990s or early 2000s, it typically operated on a £35 or £70 jackpot setup depending on the specific model cabinet and location settings.
The machine is heavily themed around a heist, a board game strategy, or a pun on "taking a piece of the action." Like most classic British "fruities" from that era, the gameplay consists of two distinct stages:

• Mahjong Showdowns: Players engage in standard Japanese mahjong matches against a lineup of female opponents.

• Punishment Mechanics: True to the franchise, winning matches triggers interactive sequences. However, 4 Ever famously added options to inflict no punishment on the opponents, showing them happy without forced nudity.

• Visual Peak: The game is widely considered by arcade enthusiasts to be the visual peak of the franchise.
Take The Piste

Take the Piste is a classic UK pub fruit machine (AWP) manufactured and released by Mazooma Games in 1998.

Within the UK fruit machine enthusiast community, Take the Piste is famously remembered as a "dump-a-lump" machine. This means its payout style was historically quite "lumpy"—frequently absorbing coins for long stretches before dumping out its jackpot or high-value token streaks all at once.
Take Your Pick

The Barcrest Take Your Pick is a classic, nostalgic UK fruit machine first released in the 1980s.

True to 1980s Barcrest designs, it relies heavily on classic nudges, holds, and feature-selection ladders where players choose to risk or collect their current winnings.
Takeda Shingen

Takeda Shingen is a 2D beat'em up game with weapons. Game is similar to its namesake on the Turbografx-16, but has some differences.

The "Sengoku" period was a time of great internal conflicts in Japan. Takeda Shingen was a famous daimyo (territorial lord) in this time - he is the game's main hero. The game is a typical beat 'em up with weapons and a scrolling screen. Controls are similar to Double Dragon II: The Revenge - with right and left attack buttons.

The title also has a between-level "minigame" - Takeda rides on his horse and must shoot a target, using his bow.
Talbot

Talbot © 1982 Volt Electronics.
Released in August 1982.

The player controls a peasant with a red pointed hat, he is a rabbit breeder and accompanied with his loyal hunting dog talbot breed, must recapture all the rabbits that have escaped and are running around the maze field. 

You must prevent the thieves with sunglasses, steal your rabbits while you avoid his attacks, it is a race against time, as you progress through the maze field you must find some food like milk to replenish your energy and give orders to your dog to put traps along the way to stop the sneaky thieves and also catch the rabbits more easy and bring them to the cage again, to go to the next round. With each round changes the maze pattern.
Tang Tang

The Associated Nexus of Galaxies (TANG) has been invaded by monsters that are going after the energy crystals. The only hope of the TANG to get the situation back to normal is to call upon four superheroes known as the Tangibles.

Tang Tang is a puzzle/action game quite similar to Solomon's Key. You control one of the four superheroes who have the ability to create and destroy blocks as well as shoot laser beams. The goal of each level is to collect all the energy crystals scattered around while avoiding the enemies. Once all the energy crystals have been collected, a door to the next level opens. Every five levels, you will have to fight against a boss.

The game boasts 120 levels although it really is 30 levels, each with four different enemy positions.
Tangram Q

Tangram Q (タングラムQ) is a puzzle arcade game by SNK heavily advertised and released in late September 1983. The game is based on the traditional game of tangram, where players could arrange pieces of a puzzle together in order to make specific shapes.
Tank

Tank is a two-player game. Each player controls a tank, and their goal is to destroy each other. However, this will be difficult, as they are located in a block maze on top of a minefield. Mines are each shown as an "X." The players move toward each other using two joysticks each, and shoot each other with a fire button on top of their right joysticks.
Tank 8

Tank 8 was produced by Kee Games (a subsidiary of Atari) in 1976.

Battle arena filled with barriers and "X"s that represent land mines is viewed from a overhead perspective by eight players who individually maneuver their uniquely colored tank in an effort to shoot the other.

Tank 8 had two modes free-for-all and team-play. In free-for-all mode you get points for every kill. In team mode, tanks were red or blue and points were scored only for killing members of the opposite team. In a design that was ahead of its time, you did have to watch out to make sure you didn't frag members of your own team.
Tank Battalion

In Tank Battalion, you control a tank in a maze. One after another, enemy tanks enter the maze, and you must shoot them all before they reach and destroy your base. The maze walls can be shot and destroyed. After all white tanks are destroyed, you proceed to the next level. Each level layout calls for different tactics, depending on the formations of the walls. Some spots on certain levels make for perfect ambush tactics, on other levels you must rally back and forth to eradicate the enemy tanks. Occasionally a red tank appears, shoot it for bonus points.
Tank Battle

Tank Battle (c) 1992 Microprose.

Trivia:
Never got past the prototype stage, JALECO acquired the division responsible for this game and scrapped the project.
Tank Busters

Tank Busters was produced by Valadon Automation in 1985.

The object of the game is to shoot all the enemy bases. To do so, you have to drive your tank through a town to find them. On your way, collect fuel before your supply runs out. The game features a top-down view.
Tank Force

Tank Force is a 2D top down arcade game. It is a sequel to Battle City, with different graphic and various details, like bigger stages or new enemies. The player controls tank and must protect the base (with eagle). He must destroy all enemy tanks on screen. The tank cannot pass through water. All buildings are destroyable, but metal walls are invincible.

Up to 4 players can play simultaneously, Player 1 controls the red tank, Player 2 controls the blue tank, Player 3 controls the yellow tank, and Player 4 controls the green tank. The game consists of 36 rounds, every fourth round also features a boss which must be defeated in addition to normal enemies.
Tank II

Tank II is the "sequel" to the arcade game Tank. The game is almost 100% identical to Tank. Two-players face off against each other, shooting each other's tanks, navigating the maze, and avoiding land mines. The difference is the levels. The maps are different due to the game being wired differently. There are no computer opponents, so two players are required to play.
Tank! Tank! Tank!

Tank! Tank! Tank! is a 2009 third-person shooter arcade game developed and published by Namco Bandai Games. Players control their respective tanks and must destroy opponents and giant mechanical monsters with a variety of weapons, such as machine guns and rocket launchers. Its gameplay has been compared to titles such as the Earth Defense Force series, through its usage of B-movie tropes and parodying.

Designed by producer Makoto Ishii, Tank! Tank! Tank! is a spiritual successor to Tokyo Wars (1996), an older Namco arcade game that shared many of the same mechanics and ideas. Ishii wanted to create an arcade game that allowed players to express themselves through its fast-paced gameplay and visuals. He designed it around a vertical-oriented monitor, a concept borrowed from the popularity of Japanese mobile games. As these were often played with a vertical screen, Ishii believed it would automatically make players familiar with the gameplay of Tank! Tank! Tank!.
Tap a Tune

Tap a Tune invites the player into a rhythm-driven arcade challenge where musical cues and timing are central. The setting is abstract: the cabinet presents the player with a sequence of beats or patterns, and the goal is to respond in time, testing reflexes and rhythm rather than narrative drama.

When the player begins, the game displays rhythmic prompts tied to the music — these may include beats, taps or visual indicators aligned to a track. The player must tap corresponding buttons or controls in synchrony with the cues. Successive sequences increase in speed or complexity, rewarding the player for precise timing and consistency. The session ends when the player’s timing windows fail or the programmed sequence completes, and a score is tallied based on accuracy and streaks of correct inputs.
Tapper

Tapper is a fixed-screen action game in which the player controls a bartender serving a growing crowd of thirsty customers. Four horizontal bars extend across the screen, each ending at a keg. Customers enter from the opposite side and gradually approach the bartender, who must fill mugs and slide them along the correct bar before anyone reaches the serving end. Clearing every customer advances to the next screen.

Moving up or down transfers the bartender between bars, with the top and bottom positions wrapping around, while moving left or right allows him to run along the current counter. Holding the serving control fills a mug, and releasing it sends the drink sliding toward the customers. Each served drink pushes its recipient farther back, but later customers may require several before leaving. Empty mugs are thrown back along the bar and must be collected before they fall from the counter.
Targ

Targ is a one or two player shooter game released by Exidy in 1980. Your town is invaded by Targ riders, you must manouvre the heroic vehicle Whummel to destroy them. From time to time, a Spectar comes into screen, and can be destroyed for extra bonus.

Action takes place into a 9x9 grid, "Crystal City", where the player's vehicle must avoid and chase down 10 enemy wedge-shaped vehicles. When all enemies are destroyed, you are awarded an extra bonus and can access the following level. Two players can alternate in the game. You use a 4 way joystick to control the Whummel, and a pushbutton to fire at enemies. Progressing in the gameplay causes the Targs to become faster and smarter, for a fast and furious gameplay.

A small trivia on the game and characters name: apparently, Targ stands for Target, Spectar stands for Special Target.
Target Ball
A classic pool shooting game with strip poker elements.
Target Ball '96

Pretty simple pool game that rewards you with a pic of a partially clothed woman after you succeed at meeting the target score for each round. Maybe they get nekkid at after so many rounds, I only got to 2 or maybe 3 pics.
Target Bravo: Operation Ghost

Target Bravo: Operation Ghost puts players in the shoes of highly trained special force agents. They must use precision shooting and quick reactions to complete the mission whilst using some of the brand new tools at their disposal in this brand new 55” LED” Upright edition of the evergreen Sega franchise! As well as new weapons, gadgets and equipment, Target Bravo: Operation Ghost allows players to start at any stage of the game, thereby encouraging them to come back and play their favourite stages again and again!

The game retains the same storyline as the original Operation G.H.O.S.T.. Taking place in 2035, the game pits the Global Humanitarian Operations & Special Tactics task force (G.H.O.S.T.) against the Blue Wolf terrorist organization.
Target Hits

Target Hits is a shooting practice game for one or two players using a light gun. It contains three fixed-screen games with several scenes for each one:

 - Shooting Range: a traditional shooting range with targets that move towards the front of the screen, either in a straight line or with circular movement. There are also skulls and those need to be avoided. At the end of each stage the amount of hits and the accuracy are shown. There are five lives and when a skull is shot or a target reaches the screen a life is lost.

 - Desert Chariots: here moving targets need to be shot on vehicles moving sideways, left and right. When all targets are destroyed the chariot explodes. Enough targets need to be shot before they leave the screen to keep progressing. The same lives system is used as in Shooting Range. There are skulls to be avoided and sometimes there is a bottle instead of a regular target.

 - Track Wagons: here a single target needs to be shot on a wagon.
Target Panic

Target Panic is an arcade target-practice shooter. The player engages a series of staged shooting scenarios in which on-screen targets appear in various patterns and speeds; the objective is to hit targets accurately to accumulate points and advance through successive stages.

Players control an on-screen aiming reticle to shoot moving and stationary targets. Points are awarded based on accuracy and target value; some targets yield bonus points or special effects. Stages present different target arrangements and pacing, and play continues until the player’s available credits or lives are exhausted.
Target Toss Pro: Bags

Target Toss Pro: Bags is an arcade video game by Incredible Technologies based on the backyard game Cornhole. A version for WiiWare co-developed by n-Space was released on November 17, 2008 in North America.

Target Toss Pro: Bags is an alternative sports video game based on the game Cornhole. Gameplay consists of throwing bean bags onto a board with a hole in it. Getting a bag inside the hole scores extra points.
Target Toss Pro: Lawn Darts
